idiom_name: grant set derived per component, held by an identity or sandbox boundary
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: for every component, derive the smallest set of rights its job needs (files, endpoints, tables, topics, syscalls, scopes), attach that set to the component's own identity at the strongest available boundary - a separate uid or service account, a container or sandbox profile, a cloud IAM role, a database grant, a framework policy - and originate the component with nothing so that the default is no authority and the grant is the only thing it has. Keep the derivation as a reviewed artifact, re-derive it when the job changes, and shape the mechanism so privilege is raised late and dropped early with the drop on every exit path (scope guard, RAII, defer, finally) instead of a call an error path can skip. What replaces the classic structure: there is no participant collaboration to instantiate - the enforcement is the identity or boundary the component runs under, so prefer kernel and platform checks to in-process ones, and treat an in-process guard as a convenience layered on top rather than the boundary itself.
code_sketch:
component = Service("reports-worker")
grants = derive_grants(component.job)      # endpoints, tables, topics, syscalls
identity = provision(component, grants)    # own uid / role / service account
with run_as(identity, read_only_fs=True, caps=[]):   # nothing to raise or drop
    component.run()                        # it never held more than the grant
# a right the job does not name is not granted, and the drop is not a call
# that an error path can skip - the component simply never had the authority
pitfalls: Deriving the grant set from what the component can reach today instead of from the job it must do: the current access becomes the baseline, the excess is inherited as normal, and nothing is ever removed.
Enforcing in process only: a guard, decorator or type check that some code path bypasses is not a boundary while the component still holds the ambient authority.

Privilege that outlives the operation: elevation that is not scoped to every exit path (CWE-250's example is an exception that skips the lowering call) or a long-lived helper that keeps its authority between requests.
Grants with no owner and no expiry: rights added for a migration or an incident stay forever, so the effective privilege set is the union of everything anybody once needed.

Wrong move: count narrow-looking RBAC roles as proof of least privilege -> inherited memberships, wildcard verbs and resource hierarchies can leave effective access broad or unreviewable -> instead enumerate effective permissions at the enforcement point and test the deny cases.

Wrong move: infer the grant set from observed successes alone -> unused or rare-path rights remain invisible, while fine-grained role mining can trade excess privilege for unreviewable configuration -> instead derive permissions from the job, bound them explicitly and review the resulting effective grant set.
